# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review of "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Varga & Holm, Comment)

**Bottom line:** The first half of this comment is valuable. The attrition finding, the comparison of manager ratings with records, and the actual-hours correction are real contributions from microdata. The second half overreaches. The headline claim, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact," is not supported by the authors' own corrected estimate. It also ignores the strongest evidence against it, the Varden case-processing result, which the comment cites selectively. In short, it mirrors the Halden paper's overreach in the opposite direction.

## Arithmetic: mostly correct, one inconsistency, one error

| Figure | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Record-based output, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.8 | +18.9% ✓ |
| Hours ratio, 27 organisations | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 (−14.1%) | ✓ |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% ✓ |
| Hours ratio, 17 organisations | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 (−13.9%) | ✓ |
| Record-based output, actual hours | 95.4 / 86.1 | +10.8% ✓ |
| Manager minus records | 98.9 − 95.1 | 3.8 points ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% ✓ |

**The hours decomposition does not add up (§3).** The authors attribute the extra hours to longer days (+0.7 hours on each of four days) plus 1.6 logged hours on the day off. That is 2.8 + 1.6 = 4.4 hours above the 32 scheduled, or about 36.4 hours a week. The reported actual figure is 34.6, only 2.6 hours above schedule. Either the components or the total is wrong, and since the actual-hours correction drives Table 2, this needs resolving.

**The novelty extrapolation is miscalculated (§6).** Energy fell from 0.61 to 0.29 SD over three months, about 0.107 SD per month. Continuing that decline linearly reaches zero at around **month 8.7**, not month ten. More importantly, a straight line through two points after a rise is not a credible model, as §4 below explains.

## 1. Selective use of the Varden trial

The comment calls Varden's counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature." But the same randomised trial, with record-based output, timesheet hours and a control group, found **+12.5% output per actual hour in case-processing offices at nine months**.

That result directly tests the comment's thesis:

- **Measurement:** output came from administrative records and hours from timesheets.
- **Selection:** offices were randomly assigned and none withdrew.
- **Novelty:** the result held at month nine, roughly where the comment's own extrapolation says enthusiasm should have run out.

The Varden case-processing result is never mentioned. Notice too that the comment's best corrected Halden estimate (+10.8%) is close to Varden's randomised estimate (+12.5%). Read together, the two studies point toward a real gain of around 10–12% per actual hour in work not tied to presence, at least up to nine months. They do not point to zero.

My earlier review of Varden raised real caveats: overtime cost, wide intervals with few clusters, and backlog. Those concern cost and precision. None of them makes the per-hour gain an artifact.

## 2. The abstract overstates what was corrected

The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems, including attrition, brings the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. **Attrition is not corrected anywhere.**

That is a gap the authors could fill. The microdata seem to contain the seven organisations that withdrew after starting. The authors could:

- bound the estimate, for example with Lee bounds or by assigning withdrawers worst-case outcomes; or
- report an intention-to-treat style figure that includes them.

The abstract should be fixed either way.

## 3. Table 2 mixes corrections with changes in sample

Each row of Table 2 uses a different subset (61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations). The step from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore combines the effect of the corrections with the effect of changing which organisations are included. For example, the manager-reported index is 98.7 for all 61 organisations but 98.9 for the 23.

All four specifications should be computed on the same 17 organisations, so readers can see how much each correction contributes. The Data Note admits that the subsets are not random, which is good. But it then contradicts the general conclusion in §8, because organisations that keep time logs and output records are probably concentrated in particular sectors.

## 4. The novelty argument is asserted, not tested

- **Wrong variable.** Self-reported energy is not output. The comment shows enthusiasm declining but never shows *productivity* declining.
- **A direct test was available.** The Halden output index was collected **monthly**, and the authors have the microdata. If novelty drives the result, record-based output per actual hour should fall from month three to month six. That test was not run.
- **The shape is ambiguous.** Energy rose from zero, peaked and then fell. That pattern fits decay toward zero equally well as settling at a positive plateau. Two points cannot tell these apart.
- **The burden of proof applies both ways.** "Not yet shown to be durable" is a fair conclusion. "Entirely an artifact" is a positive claim and needs its own evidence.

## 5. The record-based measure may be biased downward in some organisations

Records included "billable hours delivered." For professional-services firms billing by time, billable hours are partly an *input* measure. They fall mechanically when hours fall, whether or not more value is produced per hour. Part of the 3.8-point gap between managers and records may therefore reflect the measure, not managerial optimism.

The authors should report the gap separately by type of record. Notably, 19 of 23 organisations showed the gap, which a sign test puts at p ≈ 0.003, so the gap itself is solid. Its size is what is uncertain.

## 6. The meetings section mischaracterises Varden

- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known."** Varden says the meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- **"A subgroup."** The seven offices are the registered case-processing stratum's treated arm, not an ad hoc subgroup.
- **"Should not be cited as a mechanism."** Varden already said exactly this. They labelled the analysis exploratory, said a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism, and registered a confirmatory test.

The comment also ignores independent corroboration: 47 of 58 Halden managers reported cutting meetings. More fundamentally, the meetings hypothesis cuts *against* the comment's thesis. If gains come from removing low-value time, that is a real and plausibly durable productivity change, not a novelty effect. Dismissing it is convenient for the "entirely an artifact" conclusion, but no evidence is offered for the dismissal.

## 7. The attrition finding is the most serious charge and needs care

The working paper said the nine organisations withdrew "during the preparation phase." The comment says seven withdrew after the schedule had begun, six of them citing workload. If this is accurate, it is a material misdescription in the original paper, not just a limitation.

Given its weight, the comment should:
- quote the exit-form wording;
- say whether the Halden authors were asked to respond; and
- report the sectors of the withdrawing organisations. If they were mainly retail or hospitality, that sharpens §5 further.

## 8. What the evidence supports

**Supported by the comment:**
- Halden's 23.4% is substantially overstated.
- After the output and hours corrections, roughly 11% remains in the subset where those corrections can be made.
- Halden's nominal revenue figure is misleading in real terms.
- Halden's sector-general claim is an artifact of dividing by 0.8.
- Attrition, if as described, was neither random nor accurately reported.

**Not supported:**
- That the remaining gain is novelty, since output over time was not tested.
- That per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact," given the residual 10.8% and the Varden case-processing result.
- That the meetings mechanism should be dismissed.

A more defensible conclusion would be: "Corrected estimates suggest a gain in output per actual hour of roughly 10–12% in work not tied to presence, consistent with the one randomised trial. Its durability beyond nine months is untested, and in work tied to presence, reduced hours reduce output per employee."

The comment's methodological recommendations are excellent and agree with both earlier papers. Analysing all enrolled organisations, including those that withdraw, is especially important.
